Building the backtesting engine
At its core, running a backtest means trying to answer a
counterfactual question
(see chapter
Causal inference

): what would have our algorithm traded had it been executed in a past trading session? Our algorithm is sending order to the market that did not exist in the past, and we need to simulate the impact of these orders in the market. When working in
limit order book
based markets, we typically consider two different types of effects:
Instantaneous market impact

: which is the inmediate effect that our order has in the limit order book. For example, a limit order at a price where there is not an opposite matching order, will be added to the liquidity available in the order book. Alternatively, a market order will consume limit orders, removing the liquidity from the market.
Permanent market impact

: which is the effect that our orders have on future orders arriving to the market. For instance, consuming liquidity from the limit order might trigger a cascade of orders in the same side, coming from algorithms making decisions based on the shape of the order book. Another possibility is that the price movement produced by this consumption of liquidity triggers stop orders. And so on.

The ideal backtest would simulate the market impact of our orders. However, this is not feasible if we intend to stick to the historical data: once our orders alter the market dynamics, historical orders are no longer compatible with it. This becomes the real of simulated markets, which we will discuss in the next section, which bring their own issues since the simulated dynamics might not necessarily be representative enough of real market dynamics, being model dependent.

Therefore, in order to run backtests with historical data, we need to make some compromises when modelling the impact of our orders. The most simple one is completely ignore the effect of our orders in the market dynamics, i.e. neglecting both instantaneous and permanent market impact. In this
shadow
backtesting mode, we use historical data to trigger the orders from the trading algorithms, as well as to simulate their execution. For example:

We can compute the price at which a market order is executed by reconstructing the limit order book at a given time and simulating an execution against the available liquidity. This liquidity is not, however, removed from the reconstructed order book, as we proceed forward with the simulation.

Analogously, we could add our limit orders to the queue in a reconstructed order book at a certain price level, and simulate an execution against an incoming market order or agressive limit order that reaches the price level where the level sits (as well as having enough volume to reach our order a that price level). But again, the simulation continues on without considering the impact of our order.

A second feasible option is to consider the instantaneous market impact, but not the permanent one. In this case, we rely completely on keeping a reconstruction of the order book over the simulation, which is updated with our own orders. For example, if we place an order at a tick above the best bid, an incoming market order of the same volume would consume our order but leave orders are the next price levels unaltered, which is something that would not have happened in the absence of our order. However, in our simulation, we continue using the history of incoming market and limit orders (or other order types), which we assume are not affected by the impact of our orders.

As a side note, it is worth to point out that typical tick by tick datasets provide order information in the form of quotes and trades. This does not directly provide the information about the native orders that were submitted to the market. For instance, a trade could happen because of a market order or because of an aggressive limit order, to consider the most simple types of orders (see chapter
Market microstructure

). To reverse engineer the type of orders in order to consistently update our reconstruction of the limit order book, we need to make some hypotheses. A simple one maps quotes with limit orders and trades with market orders, the side of the latter being inferred comparing their price against the prevalent mid-price at the time of arrival of the order (the mid-price from the historical order books, not the reconstructed one, that might be already affected by our orders).

All this is to highlight that historical backtests are based on strong modelling assumptions and simplifications, and therefore their results need to be considered as much as optimistic bounds for the behaviour of the tested trading algorithm in real market conditions.
To close this section, let us briefly discuss the case of backtesting in
RfQ based markets

. The most typical case in this setup is that of a dealer testing trading algorithms that generate prices to respond to the RfQs from the clients. As discussed above, historical data consists on past RfQs received. The same argument regarding market impact apply in this case.  If we want to stick to the history of RfQs, we have to assume that when testing alternative pricing policies as the ones that happen in the historical data will not affect future order flows, which is equivalent to the permanent market impact discussed above. Notice that this might be also a strong hypothesis in these markets since clients might, for instance, stop sending RfQs to a dealer that consistently quotes uncompetitive prices. A similar situation might occur when simulating indicative prices quoted by dealers in streaming to electronic platforms, which might influence the incoming flow of RfQs.

The analogous to the instantaneous market impact in this setup is the actual outcome of the RfQ. From historical data the dealer knows if the client traded or not given the quoted price. There is also extra information that can be available pre and post-trade, as discussed in chapter
Market microstructure

. For instance, the client identity, instrument type, side, volume and number of competing dealers (in multi-dealer-to-client platforms) are available at the time of quoting. And afterwards, many platforms provide information about the second best price (cover) for dealers that won the RfQ, as well as information about the client trading with other dealer or simply walking away. As also discussed before, for some instruments there is information available about the prices and volume closed, typically due to regulatory requirements. This information can be used to simulate the outcome of the RfQ when using alternative pricing policies, by estimating models that predict the probability of trading given the RfQ context and the quoted price. These models will be discussed extensively in chapter
Modelling RfQs in Dealer to Client Markets
Backtesting runs and interpretation of results

children.label: Backtesting runs and interpretation of results

children.value: The results of backtesting trading algorithms and trading strategies in general have to be considered optimistic: getting good results in backtesting does not guarantee good results in a real trading environment; however, if the results of the backtesting are bad, the trading algorithm should definitely be reviewed before releasing it into production.
There are good practices and considerations, though, that help maximize the utility of a backtesting:

When running a backtesting, we need to select a period of historical data and a universe of instruments that we intend to trade. For both selections, it is convenient to follow the general data science good practice of dividing data into three sub-sets: training, validation and testing. As its name suggests, the
training set

is used to train the strategy, which might involve from selecting the parameters that maximize the performance metrics of the strategy, to learning predictive models that are used for decision making. A
validation set

is typically used to choose across different candidate strategies and models, sometimes belonging to a parametric family of them. Therefore, it is typically said that the validation set is used to choose hyperparameters. Once a final candidate is chosen, we run a final backtesting using the
testing set
, that contains data that has not been used for training and validation. The results of the backtesting on the testing set are considered the closest to the real performance of the strategy
The selection of these three datasets needs to be done carefully. A good practice is to select the training and validation sets from time periods before the testing set. This is to avoid a
look ahead bias

, in which we indirectly leak information from the future into the training and selection of the trading strategy. Given that markets show typically a strong autocorrelation, a good practice is to add some censored periods between training / validation and testing data, which are not used at all in the backtesting. This helps to reduce the effect of correlations between the different datasets.
Markets usually show different
regimes

, typically in terms of trend and volatility. If our strategies are supposed to be used in a particular regime, it is convenient to select historical data from similar regimes. This selection has to be done using the same criteria that will be used in a real trading session to select if the regime is appropriate for the operation of the strategy.

In terms of instrument selection, ideally if we intend to trade on a wide universe of instruments, it is convenient to leave entirely some instruments out of the training and validation set, unless we intend to finetune the strategy at the instrument level. In that case, we might want to train the strategy in all the instruments, but leave model and strategy selection for a subset of them. This and the previous good practices seek in the end to avoid the so-called
data snooping bias

, in which the choice of strategy is too influenced by patterns and correlations of the specific data in the testing and validation sets, which don’t generalize well to other data and instruments in the tradable universe. A related problem is that of
overfitting
, that happens when we use overparametrized models and strategies, which makes it easier for the strategy to fit the training data in a way that does not generalize well to other datasets.
Finally, particularly when performing backtesting over long time periods like years, we have to be particularly careful about
survivorship bias

, i.e. selecting only the instruments that have performed well up to today but neglecting some that did not perform well. This can happen obviously in the case of firms that become bankrupt and their stock or bonds dissappear from the market, but also when using as the universe of tradable instruments those that are currently more liquid or that belong today to a relevant index like the S&P 500 or the Euro Stoxx 50. We have to use the same logic for universe selection in the past as the one we would use in the present, to ensure we also include potential
losers
in the backtesting.
For a deeper dive into the systematics of backtesting, the book by Marcos López de Prado is a good reference
Prado, 2018
Testing in simulated markets

There are several reasons why backtesting with historical data might not provide enough safe guarantees when it comes to estimate the real performance in trading conditions. Let us summarize the main ones:
Lack of enough historical data

: there might be simply not enough data from previous trading sessions to do a comprehensive assessment, particularly for strategies that use end of day prices or even larger time intervals. The problem is compounded when we know that markets are continually changing so the older the data, the less representative might be of future trading conditions.
Indirect data snooping bias

: given the scarcity of historical data, even if we are rigorous in avoiding the biases commented in the previous section for our particular design and testing of a trading strategy, the truth is that some of these datasets are the most crowded that exist. For example, end of day data from US and European stocks belonging to the main indexes. Thousands of articles and research reports have been devoted to testing trading strategies over this data, meaning that is rare that a professional or academic working in the financial sector has not been indirectly influenced by previous results working on these datasets. This means that when testing a new trading strategy on this data, we might be likely incurring at some degree on data snooping bias.
Insufficient market feedback

: as also discussed in the previous section, we can include some limited market feedback when working with historical data, particularly around instantaneous market impact when the orders of our trading strategy are relatively marginal with respect to those of the overall market. However, the reality is that real markets will adapt to our orders, and in order to incorporate this feedback effects we need to deviate from the historical time-series.

This motivates the use of market simulators that are able to generate an unlimited number of trading scenarios and provide a comprehensive feedback mechanism. These simulators might still rely on historical data for calibration or initialization, but the role of this data ends there.

There are two major ways to build market simulations. The first one is based on estimating a generative probabilistic model for the orders in the market. The second one tries to model the behaviour of representative agents that operate in markets, which generate in turn the orders that arrive to the simulation. We will cover the simulation of dealer-to-client markets that operate with request for quotes in chapter
Modelling RfQs in Dealer to Client Markets
. Simulation of limit order book (LOB) markets is discussed in detail in
Modelling the Limit Order Book
Effects and Risks of Algorithmic Trading

children.label: Effects and Risks of Algorithmic Trading

children.value: The expansion of algorithmic trading has had significant and measurable effects on market structure, both beneficial and potentially destabilising. Understanding these effects requires separating the structural consequences of widespread algorithmic participation from the specific pathologies that can arise when algorithms malfunction or are deliberately misused.
Market Quality Effects

The most consistently documented positive effect of algorithmic trading—and of HFT market making in particular—is the compression of bid–ask spreads and the increase in quoted depth in electronic order books. By continuously quoting both sides of the market, algorithmic market makers increase the supply of immediately available liquidity, reducing transaction costs for end investors. Empirical studies across multiple asset classes confirm that the introduction of electronic and algorithmic trading has been associated with narrower spreads and lower price impact for standard-sized transactions
European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), 2019

However, this liquidity is conditional and fragile. Unlike traditional broker-dealer market makers, who historically operated under contractual or reputational obligations to maintain quotes in stressed conditions, most algorithmic liquidity providers—particularly HFT firms—face no such obligations. Empirical evidence shows that HFT market makers tend to reduce or withdraw their quotes precisely during episodes of market stress, when spreads widen and volatility spikes. This behaviour, while individually rational, can amplify price dislocations when it occurs simultaneously across many participants, creating an asymmetry between normal and stressed market conditions
Bank for International Settlements (BIS), 2018

A related effect is the ambiguous net impact of algorithmic trading on volatility. In normal conditions, deeper liquidity tends to reduce volatility. Yet the episodic withdrawal of algorithmic liquidity during stress—and the herding dynamics described below—can amplify extreme events, making the overall effect of HFT on volatility difficult to sign empirically. The literature documents lower
routine
volatility alongside an elevated incidence of short-lived but severe dislocations.

Two further structural effects deserve mention. First, the widespread use of execution algorithms—which fragment large parent orders into sequences of smaller child orders spread across time and venues—has reduced the average trade size and increased the total number of trades and messages generated in modern markets. This trade fragmentation is a defining feature of post-2005 equity microstructure data across all major exchanges. Second, relative-value and arbitrage algorithms, by rapidly exploiting price discrepancies between related instruments or across venues, contribute to
price consistency
: persistent cross-market arbitrage opportunities that once lasted minutes or hours are now compressed to milliseconds in liquid markets
Bank for International Settlements (BIS), 2018
. In this sense, algorithmic activity promotes allocative efficiency by ensuring that prices reflect information more uniformly across venues and instruments.
Systemic Risks
The same speed and interconnectedness that make algorithmic trading efficient in normal conditions become a source of systemic fragility under stress. A recurring concern is
algorithmic herding

: when many independently designed algorithms share similar data inputs, signals, or risk thresholds, they may react to market events in a highly correlated manner, amplifying price movements rather than dampening them. This self-reinforcing dynamic has been identified as a contributing factor in several episodes of sudden and severe market dislocation
European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), 2019
The
Flash Crash of 6 May 2010
remains the most studied such episode. As shown in
Figure

, the DJIA, S&P 500 Index, and E-Mini S&P 500 futures all fell sharply together around 13:30 CT before recovering within approximately 20 minutes—a dislocation that was simultaneous across instruments and almost entirely reversed, two hallmarks of algorithmically driven rather than fundamentals-driven price moves. The joint CFTC–SEC investigation concluded that a large algorithmic sell order interacted with aggressive HFT strategies that withdrew their liquidity during the stress, producing a rapid cascade that temporarily disconnected prices from fundamentals
U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission and U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, 2010
. A subsequent investigation in 2015 identified that a London-based trader, Navinder Singh Sarao, had been deploying a
layering

strategy (described below) to artificially distort the order book for S&P 500 futures immediately before the crash, illustrating how deliberate manipulation can interact with automated systems to produce extreme outcomes.

A structurally analogous episode occurred on
7 October 2016

, when sterling fell approximately six percent against the US dollar in a matter of minutes during a period of thin Asian-session liquidity before rapidly recovering. Investigations attributed the event to a combination of automated news-reading systems reacting to Brexit-related commentary, risk-management algorithms amplifying the initial move, and HFT liquidity withdrawal during the stress
Markets Committee, Bank for International Settlements, 2017

. Notably, the episode was not attributed to a single algorithmic actor, but to the interaction of multiple independent systems operating under similar stress signals—an illustration of how systemic risk can emerge from individually rational behaviour.

Because many algorithmic strategies operate simultaneously across multiple instruments and venues—multi-leg arbitrage, index replication, delta hedging— a stress event in one market can propagate almost instantaneously to others. The 2010 Flash Crash demonstrated how stresses originating in equity index futures could transmit rapidly into individual equities, exchange-traded funds, and related derivative markets within seconds, a form of cross-market contagion that is qualitatively different from the slower contagion mechanisms observed in pre-algorithmic markets.
Operational Risk

A distinct class of risk arises from algorithms that malfunction unintentionally due to implementation errors, infrastructure failures, or unanticipated market interactions. A canonical example is the
Knight Capital incident

of 1 August 2012. A production deployment error activated a legacy routing component that began submitting an uncontrolled stream of orders in more than one hundred NYSE-listed securities. Within 45 minutes, Knight Capital Group had accumulated large unintended positions and suffered losses of approximately $440 million—a sum representing a substantial fraction of the firm’s equity capital—before the errant algorithm was halted. The positions were subsequently liquidated at a significant discount, contributing to the firm’s eventual acquisition by a competitor
U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, 2013

. The incident demonstrated that the speed advantages of algorithmic trading translate equally into speed of loss when a system fails, and underscored the importance of pre-trade risk controls, kill-switch mechanisms, and disciplined production release procedures.

Operational risk in algorithmic trading is not limited to dramatic single-firm events. More routine failures—brief connectivity outages causing stale orders to linger, parameter miscalibrations causing algorithms to trade at unintended volumes, or race conditions in multi-venue routing logic—collectively represent a significant source of operational exposure for trading firms and, in aggregate, can affect market quality.

The increasing use of AI coding tools in software development poses, in this regard, a relevant risk. These tools tend to rewrite large chunks of code rather than the limited, targeted interventions that human developers typically make, enlarging the surface area of each change and making thorough review substantially harder. Without a corresponding increase in testing rigour—covering not just functional correctness but the domain-specific invariants of trading systems, such as order-size limits, position constraints, and connectivity fail-safes—AI-generated code introduces latent risk that may not surface until the algorithm is live. The Knight Capital incident is a cautionary parallel: a routine deployment change, inadequately reviewed, activated logic that should never have reached production. The speed with which AI tools generate and modify code, if not matched by proportionally stricter governance, risks increasing both the frequency and the magnitude of such episodes.
Market Abuse

Beyond unintentional malfunctions, trading algorithms can be deployed deliberately to distort or manipulate markets. European regulation identifies specific forms of algorithmic market abuse under the Market Abuse Regulation (MAR, Regulation (EU) No 596/2014)
European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2014
, and analogous prohibitions exist under U.S. securities and commodities law.
Spoofing

involves placing a large limit order on one side of the order book—typically at or near the best bid or offer—with the intent to create a false impression of supply or demand, while simultaneously submitting a genuine order on the opposite side. Other market participants, particularly algorithms that use order-book imbalance as a short-term directional signal, may react to this order by trading at prices that benefit the spoofer. The distorting limit order is then cancelled before it can be filled -which, however, could happen in the interim, making this strategy also risky. A variant of the strategy waits for the best quote to reprice in response to the spoofed order, cancels the large limit order, and then consumes the repositioned liquidity with an aggressive market order.
Layering

extends this logic by placing multiple distorting limit orders at several consecutive price levels on one side of the order book simultaneously, rather than a single large order. This creates a more convincing appearance of deep one-sided interest and is particularly effective in instruments where the natural depth at the best bid or offer is thin. The 2010 Flash Crash investigation identified layering in S&P 500 futures as a contributing trigger, and a series of enforcement actions across the U.S. and European jurisdictions has since established layering as a clearly prosecuted form of market abuse.
Banging the close

refers to executing a large number of transactions near the end of a trading session with the intent of artificially influencing the settlement or closing price, which may be used to benefit positions in related derivatives or contracts that settle against that reference price.
Front-running

involves trading on one’s own account in advance of executing a known client order, exploiting privileged access to information about forthcoming order flow. The classical form is straightforward: for example, a broker who receives a large client buy order first purchases the same instrument for its own account, executes the client order —which moves the price— and then sells at a profit. This is unambiguously prohibited under securities law in all major jurisdictions.
A more contested variant, sometimes called
electronic front-running
or
latency arbitrage

, arises from the structure of fragmented electronic markets rather than from privileged bilateral information. When a large investor routes a block order across many venues simultaneously via a smart order router, the orders arrive at different exchanges at slightly different times due to varying transmission latencies. An HFT firm co-located at the nearest exchange can detect the first arriving slice, infer that further orders are headed to more distant venues, and race ahead to those venues to trade before the investor’s orders arrive—effectively purchasing shares microseconds earlier and selling them to the investor at a marginally higher price. This mechanism is described in detail in Michael Lewis’s
Flash Boys
Lewis, 2014
, which documented how latency differences across the fragmented post-Reg NMS U.S. equity market created structural opportunities for such strategies.

The book further alleged that certain dark pools—off-exchange venues ostensibly designed to protect institutional order flow—had been configured in ways that allowed HFT firms to observe and trade against client orders; Lewis cites Goldman Sachs’s dark pool Sigma X as a specific case where investors were found to be systematically disadvantaged. Whether such practices constitute front-running in the legal sense remains contested, as they do not rely on privileged bilateral information but on publicly observable order-arrival patterns and speed advantages. Regulators have nonetheless scrutinised them closely, and the episode prompted the founding of IEX, an exchange designed to neutralise latency arbitrage by imposing an equalised 350-microsecond delay on all incoming orders.
Quote stuffing

consists of submitting a very large number of orders and cancellations in rapid succession, not to create false price signals but to saturate the message-processing capacity of competing systems. By flooding an exchange’s data feed, the perpetrating algorithm degrades the ability of rival algorithms to maintain an accurate and timely view of the order book, effectively widening their operational latency window. Unlike spoofing, the mechanism is infrastructural rather than informational: the goal is to impair competitors rather than to attract their trades. Quote stuffing is explicitly addressed under MAR
European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2014
and has been the subject of regulatory scrutiny in both European and U.S. markets.
Momentum ignition

involves placing a series of orders designed to create the appearance of directional price momentum, with the intent of triggering other market participants—particularly momentum-following algorithms and automated stop-loss systems—to trade in the same direction. Once the induced price move is underway, the manipulator rapidly reverses position to profit from the artificially generated displacement. The strategy exploits the behavioural predictability of other algorithms rather than manipulating order-book depth directly, and is therefore distinct from spoofing even though it may involve order cancellations. Its effectiveness depends on the prevalence of signal-reactive algorithms in the market, making it a form of abuse that is structurally enabled by the algorithmic nature of modern market participants.
Wash trading

refers to simultaneously buying and selling the same instrument—either through coordinated accounts or self-matching orders—to generate artificial trading volume without any genuine change in economic ownership. The resulting inflated volume creates a misleading impression of market activity and liquidity, which can attract other participants or satisfy volume thresholds required for certain index inclusions or fee tiers. Wash trading is prohibited under MAR and U.S. securities and commodities law. It has been particularly prevalent in cryptocurrency markets, where the absence of comprehensive regulation until recently, combined with low fees and fragmented venues, created conditions that made artificial volume generation both easy and economically attractive
Makarov & Schoar, 2020

Taken together, the effects and risks of algorithmic trading highlight a fundamental asymmetry: efficiency benefits are diffuse and continuous, while risks tend to be concentrated and episodic. Regulatory frameworks have responded by imposing obligations—pre-trade controls, real-time monitoring, kill switches, and mandatory record-keeping—aimed at ensuring that the speed and automation of algorithmic systems are matched by an equivalent level of oversight and accountability. These obligations are detailed in the following section.
Algorithmic Trading Regulation

The regulatory framework governing algorithmic trading has evolved in response to the structural transformation of financial markets brought about by automation. The central challenge for regulators is to preserve the efficiency benefits of algorithmic trading while mitigating the systemic and conduct risks it introduces—a balance that has led to different regulatory approaches across jurisdictions.
European Union: MiFID II and MiFIR

children.label: European Union: MiFID II and MiFIR

children.value: The most comprehensive regulatory framework for algorithmic trading was introduced in the European Union through MiFID II (Directive 2014/65/EU)
European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2014
and MiFIR (Regulation (EU) No 600/2014)
European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2014

, both of which became applicable on 3 January 2018. The framework applies to investment firms engaged in algorithmic trading—including those operating high-frequency strategies—and is detailed in Regulatory Technical Standard 6 (RTS 6)
European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), 2016
, which specifies organisational requirements. The conduct obligations specific to algorithmic manipulation are governed by the Market Abuse Regulation
European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2014
The MiFID II obligations for investment firms engaged in algorithmic trading are structured around four main areas:
Governance.

Firms must maintain documented procedures covering the full lifecycle of algorithmic strategies, from development and testing to deployment and decommissioning. Each deployed algorithm must be assigned a unique identifier that is attached to every order it generates, creating an audit trail for supervisory purposes. Firms are required to maintain an inventory of all deployed algorithms, and staff involved in algorithmic trading must demonstrate the necessary technical competence.
Testing.

MiFID II places significant emphasis on pre-deployment testing. Firms must establish dedicated test environments, physically and logically separated from production systems, in which conformance testing, adverse-scenario testing, and backtesting of all algorithms intended for production can be conducted. This requirement formalises the testing procedures described in the preceding section as a legal obligation, not merely a best practice.
Resilience.
Firms must deploy real-time monitoring systems capable of detecting anomalous behaviour in deployed algorithms and acting upon it rapidly. A critical requirement is the implementation of
kill switch

mechanisms—controls that allow the immediate halting of an individual algorithm or of the firm’s entire algorithmic order flow—a direct regulatory response to incidents such as Knight Capital. Pre-trade controls must be applied to all orders, whether generated manually or algorithmically, to prevent the submission of orders with parameters that could disrupt orderly trading—for example, orders whose size or price fall outside predefined limits. Post-trade controls must also be in place, covering order reconciliation, market and credit exposure monitoring, and surveillance for potential market abuse.
Post-deployment and ongoing oversight.

Firms are required to conduct an annual self-assessment of their algorithmic trading activities, covering both standard and high-frequency operations, and to participate in annual stress tests conducted by trading platforms to assess system resilience under high-volume and high-message-rate conditions.

Firms whose activity falls under the MiFID II definition of high-frequency trading face additional obligations. Order timestamps must be recorded at microsecond precision, the offset from Coordinated Universal Time must not exceed 100 microseconds—a standard that effectively requires atomic or GPS-linked clock synchronisation—and all orders, including cancellations and rejections, must be stored for a minimum of five years to support post-event forensic analysis. Firms whose algorithmic activity qualifies as market making under MiFID II rules are additionally required to enter into formal market-making agreements with the trading venues at which they operate, committing to providing quotes within defined parameters and under defined conditions.
In Germany, a subset of these obligations was pre-empted by the High-Frequency Trading Act
Federal Financial Supervisory Authority (BaFin), 2013

, which introduced an explicit authorisation regime for HFT firms and added a speed-based criterion ensuring that firms not genuinely engaged in high-frequency activity are not subject to the most burdensome HFT-specific requirements.
United Kingdom: Post-Brexit Framework

Following the end of the Brexit transition period on 31 December 2020, MiFID II no longer applies directly in the United Kingdom. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has incorporated the substance of the MiFID II algorithmic and HFT provisions into UK domestic law through the retained EU law mechanism. In practice, the substantive requirements for governance, testing, resilience, and HFT obligations remain closely aligned with the EU framework, though divergence may increase as the FCA develops an independent UK regulatory agenda.
United States

The United States does not have a single, comprehensive regulatory framework for algorithmic trading equivalent to MiFID II. Regulatory oversight is divided between two principal agencies according to the type of instrument traded.
The
Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)

regulates securities markets. The principal regulation affecting algorithmic trading for SEC-supervised entities—including national securities exchanges, alternative trading systems, and broker-dealers—is Regulation Systems Compliance and Integrity (Reg SCI)
U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, 2014

, which requires these entities to implement and maintain robust systems, establish business continuity plans, and report systems disruptions. Broker-dealers are additionally subject to oversight from the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), whose rules include requirements for pre-trade risk controls and supervision of algorithmic strategies.
The
Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC)
regulates derivatives markets. Since 2015, the CFTC has been developing a comprehensive framework specifically targeting algorithmic trading—Regulation Automated Trading (Reg AT)
U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, 2015

—which would impose requirements broadly similar in scope to MiFID II’s RTS 6, covering pre-trade risk controls, development and testing standards, and mandatory registration for entities engaged in automated trading. As of the time of writing, Reg AT had not been finalised, reflecting both the technical complexity of the rulemaking and the political sensitivity of imposing prescriptive obligations on trading infrastructure.
Overarching Principles

Across all three jurisdictions, the regulatory philosophy governing algorithmic trading rests on several shared principles. First, the speed and automation of algorithmic systems must be matched by equivalent speed and automation of risk controls: kill switches, pre-trade limits, and real-time monitoring are not discretionary but mandatory. Second, the accountability of the human principals behind algorithmic systems must be preserved: governance obligations, unique algorithm identifiers, and record-keeping requirements ensure that automation does not create gaps in supervisory oversight. Third, the potential for algorithmic systems to be used for market abuse must be addressed through both ex ante controls—surveillance systems, order flagging—and ex post enforcement, supported by the granular data generated by the record-keeping requirements.

For practitioners, these obligations translate into significant compliance costs and operational complexity. Testing environments, atomic clocks, five-year data archives, and annual self-assessments represent substantial investments. At the same time, they align closely with the operational best practices that responsible algorithmic trading firms would adopt in any case—because the cost of failing to detect a misbehaving algorithm, as the Knight Capital episode demonstrated, can far exceed the cost of prevention.
